summary: Gathers information relevant to the development of interfaces between the telephone network and the Internet, in the PINT working group's early work. It describes implementations before the formal protocol work. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This looks at early ways to let a phone call and the internet work together, like building a bridge between two towns.

questions: how did the pstn and internet first interwork
subtitle: Early systems for combining Internet requests with telephone network calls.

tldr.problem: Web users want telephone calls and faxes triggered from Internet applications, but the PSTN and Internet were designed separately with no standard way to connect them.
tldr.mechanism: Four companies independently built pre-PINT systems that use an Internet-facing gateway to receive requests and instruct the PSTN's Intelligent Network components to execute services like click-to-dial-back and voice-access-to-content.
tldr.outcome: These implementations proved the concept works but do not interoperate because each uses a different protocol. The PINT working group later defined standard protocols for this bridge.

today: RFC 2458 is informational. It documents early implementations that proved PSTN/Internet integration was possible but used incompatible protocols. Later PINT working group documents (RFC 2848 and others) established standard protocols, with SIP becoming the primary choice for signaling on the Internet side.

sections.title: Introduction and PINT Services
sections.content:
The PSTN/Internet Inter-Networking (PINT) Working Group set out to define standard interfaces for Internet applications to request services from the Public Switched Telephone Network. This document gathers information from several companies that built systems before formal standards existed.

Four main services were identified: click-to-dial-back (a web user requests a call from an agent), click-to-fax (send a fax from the web to a PSTN fax machine), click-to-fax-back (receive a fax from the PSTN to your email), and voice-access-to-content (hear web information read aloud by phone).

The common pattern: the Internet carries the request and control messages, while the PSTN carries the voice and fax (the most important content). This split lets each network do what it does well—the Internet handles flexible user interaction, the PSTN handles high-quality voice and universal reach.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone network is very good at voice calls. The Internet is very good at showing information and taking commands. So people wanted to click on a website and have the phone network make a call.

sections.title: Common Architecture
sections.content:
All pre-PINT systems follow a similar pattern, shown in Figure 5 of the RFC. An Internet node (web server or client) sends a service request to a PINT Gateway (or directly to a Service Node in the PSTN's Intelligent Network). The gateway translates the request into PSTN terminology and instructs an Intelligent Network component—such as a Service Node or Service Control Point—to set up the call.

The Intelligent Network then acts normally: it initiates two separate calls (from the Service Node or Service Control Point to each called party) and connects them, just as it would if triggered from a telephone.

This architecture decouples Internet and PSTN interfaces. The PINT Gateway handles the Internet side; the Intelligent Network handles the PSTN side. Management and authentication happen on the Internet side, using familiar HTTP and SNMP tools.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway sits between two worlds. One side talks to websites. The other side talks to the phone network's intelligent machinery. It translates requests from one language to the other.

sections.title: IN-Based Solutions: Lucent and Siemens
sections.content:
The Lucent system uses the PSTN's Intelligent Network (IN) service node architecture. A web server accepts HTTP requests and forwards them to a Service Node via an XML-based interface, which in turn instructs a Central Office to set up calls. A Service Management System (SMS) running on the Internet manages the Service Node, letting administrators define which requests are allowed and how to handle them.

Siemens built a Web Call Center that combines a call center with web integration. When a user clicks a button on a website, a call server queues the request. An interactive voice response system (IVR) or live agent answers with appropriate prompts and handling. The implementation uses SNMP MIBs (Management Information Bases) to gather resource and job information.

Both systems proved that click-to-dial-back and similar services are feasible with the existing Intelligent Network infrastructure. The key insight is that the Intelligent Network's abstraction (service triggers and responses) maps well to internet-based requests.
sections.plainLanguage: These companies used the phone network's built-in smart features (the Intelligent Network) to handle calls. A web form becomes a service request that the phone network understands.

sections.title: Alternative Approaches: AT&T and Nortel
sections.content:
AT&T and Nortel explored alternatives to IN-based approaches. Instead of translating web requests into Intelligent Network service definitions, they built CallBroker and SCTP (Simple Computer Telephony Protocol) systems that send lower-level call control directives to Central Offices. These directives specify call states and connections directly, rather than invoking named services.

This approach is closer to how a telephone operator would direct a switchboard. Instead of saying 'invoke service click-to-dial-back with these parameters,' the gateway says 'connect party A to party B' at a more granular level. It offers direct control but requires more detailed understanding of PSTN internals.

Both approaches work, illustrating a trade-off: service-oriented (IN-based) versus command-oriented (direct control) models of interaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Some companies told the phone network 'connect these two people' directly. Others asked it to run a named service. Both work, but the direct way is like steering a car while the service way is like hailing a taxi.

sections.title: Session Initiation Protocol as an Emerging Standard
sections.content:
The document notes that the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) was emerging as a potential standard for PINT. SIP, defined for Internet multimedia sessions, offers a unified protocol for invite and control messages that can carry call setup details and user information in a standardized way.

Unlike the pre-PINT systems, which varied widely in their protocol choices, SIP provides a common language for Internet-based call signaling. It is simple, text-based (like HTTP), and extensible through headers. This made SIP the natural choice for formal PINT standards (RFC 2848 and successors), eventually enabling true interoperability between different vendors' implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The companies realized they needed a common language. SIP is that language for the Internet side of call setup, like how HTTP is the language for web browsers and servers.
